paragraphs: This paper applies a neural network trained by backpropagation to commodity trading decisions. The intended output is a long or short market position, expressing which direction the system expects to be profitable. The learning problem is therefore framed around a trading decision rather than simply producing a numerical price forecast.

The network uses fundamental and technical variables as inputs and learns their relationship to the desired trading position. The supplied abstract identifies 18 fundamental variables and gives the technical-variable count as 6 or 18. Training uses one year of historical data. The approach treats these different sources of market information as inputs to a single learned decision rule.

The abstract reports that the predicted positions would have produced $10,301 in profit from an investment below $1,000. Its wording describes a calculated trading outcome, rather than establishing that the profit was realized in live trading. The contribution is an application of supervised neural learning to connecting market indicators with directional commodity positions.
neurips-1990-a-b-p-ann-commodity-trader-.tldr: A backpropagation network learns commodity trading positions from market variables and reports a profitable calculated trading outcome.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to train a learning system made of several interacting modules. Such an architecture raises a question beyond how any one component learns: how can different learning procedures be described together so that their cooperation becomes part of the system's design? The authors propose a common framework for this purpose.

Their approach uses a statistical formulation of learning systems. Within that formulation, they describe both established connectionist algorithms and more complex architectures in which several algorithms interact. A shared mathematical language makes the relationships among these learning procedures explicit, allowing individual methods and their combinations to be considered within the same account.

The framework also supports hybrid systems that combine connectionist methods with other learning algorithms. Its stated contribution is a way to design and describe such combinations so that they can draw on the advantages of their components. The emphasis is on organizing learning across an architecture, extending the scope of analysis from an isolated algorithm to a cooperating collection.
neurips-1990-a-framework-for-the-coopera.tldr: A statistical framework gives interacting learning algorithms a common formalism for training modular and hybrid systems.

paragraphs: This paper connects the Lagrangian formulation of mechanics with the design of neural network dynamics for optimization. The central question is how to derive rules for a system's evolution so that its motion serves an optimization objective. The authors introduce a way to obtain dissipative dynamics, meaning dynamics that can settle rather than continue moving indefinitely.

The method provides a common starting point for both familiar and new neural network update rules. As a demonstration, the authors derive standard descent dynamics, which move a system toward lower objective values. Recovering this established behavior shows how an ordinary optimization procedure fits within the proposed mechanical formulation.

The same derivation also produces nonstandard variants that introduce a computational attention mechanism. This makes the formulation useful as a source of alternative dynamics as well as an explanation of existing ones. The contribution is a principled route from a mechanical description to optimizing neural behavior, with attention appearing as a feature of some resulting dynamics.
neurips-1990-a-lagrangian-approach-to-fi.tldr: A Lagrangian formulation derives familiar optimization dynamics and new neural dynamics incorporating computational attention.

paragraphs: The paper models motion computation in primate visual area MT by working across several spatial and temporal scales. Scale matters because a motion estimate can be wrong when movement is too large relative to the spacing and timing of measurements. The model addresses both the scale used to measure local velocity and the scale used to assemble a motion field.

The first stage measures local velocities through multiple channels. The second uses direction-selective neurons at several spatial resolutions to estimate optical flow, the pattern of movement across the image. It incorporates the computational efficiency of multigrid algorithms into a parallel network and adaptively combines information across scales to obtain a reliable estimate.

Multiple channels can disagree, so the authors add a veto mechanism to resolve conflicting measurements. They report that model neurons reproduce nonclassical receptive-field properties of a particular class of MT neurons. The conflict-resolution mechanism also offers an explanation for how the perceptual phenomenon of motion capture depends on spatial frequency, connecting the computational design with neural and perceptual observations.
neurips-1990-a-multiscale-adaptive-netwo.tldr: A multiscale motion network combines velocity measurements and resolves conflicts to explain properties of MT neurons and motion capture.

paragraphs: ALCOVE is a neural network model intended to explain how people learn categories. Its architecture draws on established psychological theory and is related to radial basis function networks. The goal is to build a learning system whose organization reflects ideas about human categorization, so its behavior can be compared with human learning data.

From a psychological perspective, the model combines exemplar-based representation with error-driven learning. Exemplar-based representation organizes category knowledge around examples, while error-driven learning changes the model in response to mistakes. Combining these ideas connects what the system represents with how that representation contributes to learning category judgments.

From a neural network perspective, ALCOVE places psychologically motivated constraints on a backpropagation architecture. The abstract reports that it fits a broad range of human learning data. That finding supports the usefulness of building psychological commitments into the network's design: the resulting architecture serves as a computational account of category learning, linking an explicit representation of examples with a mechanism for learning from errors.
neurips-1990-alcove-a-connectionist-mode.tldr: ALCOVE combines exemplar-based representation and error-driven neural learning to account for a broad range of human category-learning data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an attractor neural network as a common model of recall and recognition. Recall involves retrieving remembered material, while recognition involves identifying material as previously encountered. Modeling both within one architecture asks whether a shared memory mechanism can account for these different forms of access.

The authors report that the model qualitatively explains a wide range of psychological observations. These include effects associated with list length, word frequency, presentation time, changes in context, and aging. The breadth of these phenomena matters because the model is being assessed against several influences on memory rather than a single isolated effect.

The paper then estimates the probabilities of successful recall and recognition. This extends the account from reproducing qualitative patterns toward quantities that could support further numerical evaluation. The abstract presents those estimates as a basis for possible quantitative examination. Its stated result is therefore a broad qualitative account of memory access, accompanied by a step toward testing how closely the model's success rates match observed behavior.
neurips-1990-an-attractor-neural-network.tldr: An attractor network qualitatively explains several recall and recognition phenomena and estimates their probabilities of success.

paragraphs: The paper introduces bumptrees, geometric data structures for learning, representing, and evaluating relationships from samples. Their intended uses include function approximation, classification regions, constraint surfaces, and probability densities. The common problem is how to organize geometric information so that it can be constructed, accessed, and modified efficiently.

A bumptree organizes a collection of functions over a Euclidean space in a complete binary tree. Each leaf corresponds to one of the functions, and internal nodes also have associated functions. The authors describe the structure as a generalization of several hierarchical geometric representations, including oct-trees, k-d trees, balltrees, and boxtrees.

For function approximation, the approach is related to radial basis function networks, while supporting faster construction and access and more flexible modification. The paper presents an empirical comparison on a robot arm mapping task and outlines additional applications. Its central contribution is thus a reusable organization for geometric learning, linking the representation of learned functions with the efficiency of operations performed on them.
neurips-1990-bumptrees-for-efficient-fun.tldr: Bumptrees organize geometric functions hierarchically to support efficient learning, access, and modification across several learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how cholinergic modulation might improve associative memory in piriform cortex, a region involved in olfaction. It combines neuropharmacological experiments with a computational model. The approach connects a measured change in synaptic transmission with a test of what that change could mean for memory function.

The experiments examine carbachol, an analogue of acetylcholine. The authors find that it selectively suppresses transmission between cells within piriform cortex while leaving incoming connections unaffected. This selectivity is central to the proposed mechanism: the modulation changes communication within the cortical network without applying the same suppression to its inputs.

The authors then apply that pattern of suppression during learning in a model of piriform cortex. Associative memory performance improves in the model. Together, the experimental and computational findings support the possibility that selective modulation of internal connections can enhance memory formation. The biological result establishes the selective synaptic effect, while the modeling result supplies its proposed functional significance for associative learning.
neurips-1990-cholinergic-modulation-may-.tldr: Experiments and modeling suggest that selectively suppressing internal cortical connections during learning can improve associative memory.

paragraphs: The paper presents a large-vocabulary continuous speech recognizer built from linked predictive neural networks. These networks predict speech frames, and the differences between predictions and observed frames provide distortion measures. A One Stage dynamic time warping algorithm uses those measures to recognize speech across time.

This design gives the neural networks a predictive role within the recognition system. Their contribution is to assess how well speech observations fit predictions, while the time-warping procedure handles the sequence-level recognition process. The authors report that the system had already been deployed within a speech-to-speech translation system, connecting the proposed architecture to an operating application.

Reported word accuracies are 95%, 58%, and 39% on tasks with perplexities of 5, 111, and 402, respectively. The system outperforms several simple hidden Markov models tested by the authors, while its accuracy varies substantially across those tasks. Carefully chosen hidden control inputs also provide small improvements in speed and accuracy. These results establish predictive networks as a workable component of continuous speech recognition.
neurips-1990-continuous-speech-recogniti.tldr: Linked predictive neural networks supply speech-frame distortion scores for a deployed continuous speech recognizer that outperforms several tested simple HMMs.

paragraphs: This paper models memory access from multiple cues as finding the overlap between sets of possible targets. Each cue activates candidate memories, and the desired result belongs to the intersection of those sets. The authors propose this as an alternative to search-based accounts, motivated by evidence against search as the access process.

They develop two ways to compute the intersection. One uses information about the possible targets themselves. The other imposes constraints on the strengths linking cues to targets in the memory matrix. These approaches place the information needed for successful retrieval in different parts of the representation, while pursuing the same operation of identifying shared targets.

Mathematical analysis with orthogonal vectors establishes the competence of both methods under that representation. Simulations then test the second method with sparse distributed representations on tasks involving two and three cues. The combination connects an idealized analysis with distributed network behavior, showing how several cues can jointly access a memory through an intersection computation.
neurips-1990-direct-memory-access-using-.tldr: A connectionist memory model retrieves targets from multiple cues by computing the intersection of the targets each cue activates.

paragraphs: The paper develops a neural representation for recursively structured objects such as sentences. It works within harmonic grammar, which assumes that a sentence's linguistic well-formedness can be measured by the harmony, or negative energy, of its network state. This makes a numerical property of a connectionist representation stand for a linguistic judgment.

Starting from a lower-level network that satisfies a few general principles, the authors construct a higher-level network with an equivalent harmony function. The higher-level account captures global properties that matter linguistically while leaving much of the lower-level implementation unspecified. Preserving harmony connects the two descriptions through the quantity used to assess well-formedness.

The technical contribution extends tensor product representations so that they can represent fully recursive structures in the lower-level network. Recursive representation allows structured parts to contain further structured parts, as sentences do. The authors support the technique with theory and an example, demonstrating its use for parallel distributed structure processing and linking nested linguistic organization to connectionist computation.
neurips-1990-distributed-recursive-struc.tldr: An extension of tensor product representations lets connectionist networks process recursive structures while preserving a harmony-based account of linguistic well-formedness.

paragraphs: The paper studies how learning within individuals affects evolution across a population of neural networks. It examines the Baldwin effect through simulations on a pattern recognition problem. The main question is how the amount of training, and its distribution among individuals, changes the speed at which the population's genes evolve.

The simulations show that both no learning and excessive learning lead to slow genetic evolution, with an intermediate amount producing the fastest progress. This means that increasing individual training does not produce a steadily increasing evolutionary benefit. In the studied setting, the balance between learning and evolution matters more than maximizing the learning allocated to each individual.

The distribution of training also matters. With the total number of training presentations held fixed, evolution is fastest when individuals within a generation receive different numbers of presentations. The authors further connect hybrid learning and genetic algorithms with difficult, high-dimensional pattern recognition, citing the ability of genetic algorithms to help avoid local minima. Training allocation is therefore an important design choice in the combined system.
neurips-1990-evolution-and-learning-in-n.tldr: Neural-network simulations find that intermediate learning and unequal training allocations can accelerate genetic evolution.

paragraphs: The paper studies how cones remain useful across large changes in ambient illumination despite having a limited intensity-response range at any one time. The authors find that adding illumination around a cone's central stimulus shifts its response curve along the light-intensity axis. This suggests a role for surrounding illumination in setting the cone's operating range.

They investigate feedback from horizontal cells to cones as a mechanism for aligning sensitivity with peripheral light levels. To model a cone's static behavior, they construct an equivalent electrical circuit with leakage, photocurrent, and feedback channels. This provides a way to examine how the feedback synapse interacts with the cone's own light-sensitive conductance.

SPICE simulations show that those interactions can shift the intensity-response curve. The result depends on a stated condition: phototransduction must remain unsaturated during the maximally hyperpolarized light response. The model therefore offers a specific, conditional explanation for how retinal feedback can contribute to light adaptation alongside mechanisms located within the cone itself.
neurips-1990-feedback-synapse-to-cone-an.tldr: A cone circuit model shows how horizontal-cell feedback can shift light sensitivity, provided phototransduction remains unsaturated.

paragraphs: The paper develops neural network simulations of the dragonfly's flight control system to understand its use of complex, unsteady aerodynamics. The modeling task connects activity inside neural ganglia with the motor-neuron firing patterns that drive wing muscles. This places neural coordination at the center of the account of flight control.

The networks incorporate the spatial arrangement of cells, each neuron's physiological operating range, and its stochastic firing history. Training targets include both internal cellular activity and motor-neuron patterns described as flight command sequences. Using both levels of activity ties the internal network behavior to the output patterns involved in controlling flight.

The authors report that the trained networks accurately reproduce intraganglionic firing patterns, which in turn control the motor-neuron patterns driving the wing musculature. They present these networks as tools for neurobiological analysis and as initial controllers for exploiting unsteady aerodynamics. The result connects a biologically informed simulation of neural activity with a possible engineering use for the resulting control organization.
neurips-1990-flight-control-in-the-drago.tldr: Biologically informed neural simulations reproduce dragonfly firing patterns that coordinate motor activity for flight.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a radial basis function network that learns through both memorization and parameter adjustment. Its structure can grow as training proceeds. When the network encounters a pattern it handles poorly, it adds a computational unit that memorizes the desired response to that pattern, giving the difficult example a new place in the representation.

When the network already performs well on an example, it updates existing parameters using least-mean-squares gradient descent. Performance on the current pattern therefore determines which learning operation is used. The method combines a direct response to poorly represented cases with gradual refinement of knowledge already captured by the network.

The authors evaluate the approach on prediction of the Mackey–Glass chaotic time series. They report much faster learning than networks trained by backpropagation while using a comparable number of synapses. In that task, the speed advantage accompanies similar connection counts. The finding supports combining selective network growth with gradient-based adjustment as a way to make learning more efficient.
neurips-1990-leaning-by-combining-memori.tldr: A radial basis function network adds units for poorly handled patterns and refines familiar ones, learning a chaotic prediction task faster than backpropagation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses slow learning when multilayer perceptrons approximate nonlinear functions with complicated local structure. The authors attribute this difficulty to the global nature of their function approximations. Their proposed response is to incorporate B-splines into node computations, giving the network a broader set of ways to represent a function.

The resulting formulation includes ordinary multilayer perceptrons as a special case. This relationship allows the authors to develop spline network architectures within a framework that also contains familiar feedforward networks. The aim is to combine the generalization and scaling properties of global networks with the computational efficiency and learning speed associated with local computation.

The paper presents simulations on the spiral problem to demonstrate the effectiveness of the Spline Net approach. The significance is the architectural connection between global and local approximation: these become features that can be combined through the node formulation. The reported demonstration supports using spline-based computations to address learning problems whose structure varies in complex ways across the input space.
neurips-1990-multi-layer-perceptrons-wit.tldr: Spline networks generalize multilayer perceptrons to combine global approximation properties with efficient local computation.

paragraphs: This paper revisits a grid task used to illustrate temporal-difference planning and asynchronous dynamic programming. Its focus is the representation of the input stimulus: how information about the task is encoded before the learning and planning process uses it. The study asks how changing that encoding affects performance on the navigation problem.

The authors examine a particular hidden-unit representation learned through self-supervision. This introduces a learned intermediate representation between the supplied stimulus and the system's task processing. The representation itself becomes something that the system acquires, making input coding part of the learning problem rather than only a fixed design choice.

The reported finding is that learning this hidden representation improves performance. That result gives representation learning a concrete role within the grid-task setting: the information available to the planner becomes more useful through the way it is encoded. The paper's contribution is to show that the performance of this temporal-difference planning task depends on the learned internal representation as well as the planning procedure.
neurips-1990-navigating-through-temporal.tldr: Self-supervised learning of a hidden representation improves performance on a grid task for temporal-difference planning.

paragraphs: The paper applies neural networks to fault diagnosis in digitally controlled vehicle powertrains. The motivation is the difficulty of diagnosing failures in complex systems that must operate in real time. The authors report that neural networks can successfully perform this diagnostic task, treating fault identification as a learned classification problem.

A central part of the work concerns building the databases used for training and testing. These data support two linked decisions: choosing a suitable network architecture and estimating how accurately it will classify new samples. The emphasis on new data makes evaluation part of the engineering method, alongside the construction and training of the network.

The paper also presents work on neural networks for adaptive control of an active suspension system. Together, the applications address both recognizing problems in a vehicle system and adjusting its control behavior. The contribution combines an applied demonstration of powertrain diagnosis with a data-development methodology for selecting networks and assessing their expected classification performance.
neurips-1990-neural-network-application-.tldr: Neural networks diagnose powertrain faults, supported by training and testing databases, with additional work on adaptive suspension control.

paragraphs: The paper studies the computational power of threshold circuits through geometry. It represents each Boolean function of n variables as a vector with one coordinate for each possible input. This turns questions about which functions a circuit can implement into problems that can be approached using linear algebra and linear programming.

The framework yields several kinds of bounds. These concern spurious memories in Hopfield networks, the number of functions available to circuits of a given depth, and the input functions needed to construct a threshold function. It also gives a lower bound on the error of approximating Boolean functions with sparse polynomials, connecting circuit representation with approximation quality.

A further result limits a correlation-based method for proving circuit-depth lower bounds. The authors construct representations in which polynomially many input functions jointly implement a target even though none is significantly correlated with it individually. This exposes a weakness of judging representational power through individual correlations. The geometric approach also generalizes earlier results and supplies simpler proofs based on elementary linear algebra.
neurips-1990-on-the-circuit-complexity-o.tldr: A geometric view of Boolean functions yields threshold-circuit bounds and exposes limits of correlation-based complexity arguments.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a connectionist planning method for an initially unknown environment. As the system interacts with that environment, it progressively learns a world model using gradient descent. The model provides a learned basis for considering the consequences of actions, linking experience in the environment with subsequent planning.

Planning proceeds in two stages. An experience network first proposes a plan. The system then refines that proposal by gradient descent through a chain of world models, seeking actions that produce favorable future reinforcement. The initial proposal and its optimization have distinct roles: one supplies a candidate course of action, while the other adjusts it using predicted consequences.

The authors demonstrate the method on a robotics application and a pole-balancing task. These examples support the use of a learned world model as part of the planning process. The approach joins model learning, plan proposal, and plan refinement in one system, allowing experience to shape both its account of the environment and the actions selected for future reward.
neurips-1990-planning-with-an-adaptive-w.tldr: A planner learns an environment model, proposes plans with an experience network, and refines them through predicted future reinforcement.

paragraphs: The paper uses simple models from physics to investigate spatial organization in visual cortex. It focuses on ocular dominance columns and iso-orientation patches, patterns associated with eye preference and visual orientation. The question is whether compact mathematical systems can generate structural properties resembling those seen in cats and primates.

The authors use the ANNNI and Heisenberg XY spin models, with long-range interactions arranged according to a Mexican Hat operator. The interaction pattern is a central modeling ingredient: it specifies how different locations influence one another as the spatial organization forms. The approach brings established physical models into the study of cortical pattern development.

The stated finding is that these models can generate many characteristic structural properties of the cortical patterns. This supports the usefulness of simple interaction-based accounts for understanding their organization. The result concerns the ability to reproduce spatial structure, showing that a relatively compact model can capture multiple features of the patterns observed in visual cortex.
neurips-1990-simple-spin-models-for-the-.tldr: Simple spin models with Mexican Hat interactions reproduce several structural features of visual cortical columns and orientation patches.

paragraphs: This paper summarizes the aims and early results of the SPRINT project, which investigates neural computing approaches to speech recognition. The project addresses several unresolved problems within speech processing. Its scope spans different recognition tasks, giving a view of how connectionist methods can contribute at more than one level of a speech system.

The reported initial work uses feedforward networks for phonetic-unit classification, isolated-word recognition, and speaker adaptation. These tasks concern different aspects of the problem: identifying speech units, recognizing separately spoken words, and adapting to differences between speakers. Considering them together connects the representation of speech sounds with word-level decisions and variation in who is speaking.

The contribution is a project-level account of applying neural networks across those challenges. The first results establish the areas in which the approach is being explored, with feedforward networks providing the shared computational method. This breadth matters because speech recognition requires useful representations and decisions across several related tasks, and the project examines neural methods across that range.
neurips-1990-speech-recognition-using-co.tldr: The SPRINT project explores feedforward neural networks for phonetic classification, isolated-word recognition, and speaker adaptation.

paragraphs: The paper models how learning about a stimulus extends to other stimuli that may have similar consequences. Starting from Shepard's generalization theory, the authors derive a multilayer network whose units represent spherical regions with adjustable centers and radii. Learning can therefore change both where a region lies and how broadly it extends.

The model uses a Cauchy mass function and extends a configural-cue network in several ways. Combinations of cues can be learned without prewiring every possible combination, and consequential regions are continuous rather than discrete. The authors also show that the global extent of the Cauchy function increases competition among receptive fields.

They compare the approach with Gaussian mass functions and standard backpropagation networks using hyperplane or logistic hidden units. The abstract reports that those alternatives fare less well as models of human generalization and learning. The contribution connects a psychological theory to adjustable geometric representations, with the choice of mass function affecting how regions compete and how learning generalizes.
neurips-1990-spherical-units-as-dynamic-.tldr: Learnable spherical regions with a Cauchy mass function model human generalization while supporting learned cue combinations and stronger receptive-field competition.

paragraphs: The paper examines how neural networks represent both static patterns and associations across time when signals arrive with widely varying delays. This brings spatial pattern storage and temporal relationships into the same analysis. The distribution of delays is part of the system being studied, making timing central to its computational behavior.

For a particular class of these networks, the authors introduce a Lyapunov functional that makes the spatiotemporal computation easier to understand. This mathematical construction supports analysis of the network's long-run behavior. It provides a route from a system with delayed interactions to a quantitative description using statistical mechanics.

The authors derive analytical calculations for retrieval quality and storage capacity, then compare them with simulation results. These quantities address how successfully stored information can be recovered and how much the system can store. The contribution combines an explanatory mathematical tool with measurable properties of memory performance, within the class of delayed networks for which the functional applies.
neurips-1990-statistical-mechanics-of-te.tldr: A Lyapunov functional enables statistical-mechanical analysis of retrieval and storage in neural networks with distributed signal delays.

paragraphs: The paper applies KBANN, a hybrid symbolic and neural learning system, to recognizing eukaryotic splice junctions in DNA sequences. It begins with inference rules that provide an approximately correct recognition method. These rules supply prior knowledge about the task, giving the learning system an initial account of which sequences belong to the target class.

The authors map this domain theory into a neural network and then train it on examples. Learning adjusts the knowledge encoded by the rules so that the resulting network classifies the sequences properly. This creates a path from explicit symbolic knowledge to a representation that can be revised through data.

A molecular genetics experiment demonstrates the value of incorporating that preexisting knowledge. The broader methodological contribution is the conversion of an imperfect rule-based theory into a trainable network. The approach makes prior knowledge a starting point for adaptation: rules organize the initial solution, while examples help correct it for the classification task at hand.
neurips-1990-training-knowledge-based-ne.tldr: KBANN converts approximate DNA recognition rules into a neural network and refines them with training examples.
